I am fifty-seven years old. I have never been to school, but I have farmed this land in Quzhou since I was a young girl. My parents taught me, and now my bones know the seasons better than any book. I have three mu of flat, good land, and I do what every family around here does: wheat in autumn, maize in summer. That is the only way that makes sense on the North China Plain.

My wheat is already in the ground. I sowed it last October after the National Day holiday, using an improved variety I bought from the seed cooperative in town. Now it is April, and the wheat is greening up after the winter sleep. I will irrigate it four times before harvest: once now for the green-up, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, once at heading when the ears come out, and once more when the grain is filling. I already put down compound fertilizer and some manure at sowing, but I will topdress with urea when I irrigate at jointing. I spray four times total — herbicide once to keep the weeds down, insecticide twice for the aphids and armyworms, and fungicide once if the weather turns damp. I plowed the land with a rotary tiller before sowing the wheat. I expect about 1,000 jin of wheat per mu, which is what I usually get if the spring rains do not fail.

In early June, when the wheat turns golden, I will hire the combine harvester. The very same day or the next, I plant summer maize. There is no time to rest — the season is tight. I buy hybrid maize seeds, usually Nongda or Denghai brands, one small packet per mu. I do not till the land for maize; I sow directly into the wheat stubble so the soil does not dry out. I put down compound fertilizer at planting. I irrigate twice: once when the seedlings are small if June is dry, and once at the big trumpet stage when the tassels come out. I spray four times for maize too — herbicide, insecticide, and sometimes fungicide. I expect about 1,200 jin of maize per mu. The maize will be ready by late September or early October, and then the cycle starts again.

I use plenty of fertilizer because the land has been farmed for generations and needs feeding. For wheat, I use compound fertilizer and top up with urea. For maize, compound fertilizer is enough. My husband and I do most of the work by hand or with our small tractor, but we hire machines for the heavy jobs. I grow wheat and maize because they are safe — we can eat them, feed them to our animals, and sell what is left. Cotton is too much labor for these hands now, and vegetables are risky. This is how I have always done it, and this is how I will do it this year.
